title: Hand Reading in Online Poker: A Guide for Canadians
excerpt: Hand reading separates winning online poker players from breakeven ones. Here is how Canadian players can build and narrow ranges street by street.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Ask a winning online poker player what actually makes them money and you will rarely hear about bluffs or big folds. You will hear about hand reading — the unglamorous process of working out what an opponent could plausibly be holding and narrowing that set of hands street by street until your decision becomes obvious. It is the core skill of the game, it is entirely learnable, and it is the thing most recreational Canadian players never seriously practise.

Hand reading online is different from hand reading live. You cannot see a shaking hand or a tightened jaw. What you have instead is position, bet sizing, timing, and the accumulated evidence of every previous hand that player has shown down. That turns out to be plenty.

Stop thinking in hands, start thinking in ranges

The single biggest shift is to stop asking what does he have and start asking what could he have. Nobody plays a fixed hand; opponents arrive at each decision point holding one of many possible combinations, and your job is to describe that set as accurately as you can.

A range is just a list. When a tight regular opens from under the gun at a nine-handed table, their range might be something like pairs from sevens up, ace-jack and better, king-queen and a handful of suited connectors. That is roughly 10% of all hands. When the loose recreational player in the cutoff opens, their range might be 35% of hands and include every suited ace, every broadway card and any pair.

Those two ranges interact completely differently with a flop of nine-seven-two with two hearts. Against the tight opener, that board misses almost everything they hold. Against the loose player, it connects with a wide swath of their range. Same board, same cards in your hand, opposite correct play. Until you are thinking in ranges, you cannot see that difference.

Building the preflop range

Every hand read starts before the flop, and it starts with three inputs:

  • Position. Ranges widen dramatically as the action moves closer to the button. An early-position raise is always stronger than a button raise from the same player.
  • Action. Opening, calling an open, three-betting and calling a three-bet produce four completely different ranges. A cold-call is usually the most capped — very strong hands typically raise.
  • Player type. A tight regular, a loose recreational player and a maniac are three different range functions. Assign every opponent to a rough type within the first orbit.

Online, you have a fourth input the live player lacks: the sheer volume of hands. Even a short session gives you dozens of observations per opponent at a full table. Pay attention to showdowns — every hand a player turns over is a free data point about how wide they are playing from a given seat.

Narrowing on the flop

Once the flop lands, ask which part of the opponent's preflop range actually connects. Split their holdings into four buckets: strong made hands, medium made hands, draws, and air. Then watch what they do.

A small continuation bet on a dry, disconnected board usually means the whole range is betting — that sizing costs little and denies equity, so it tells you almost nothing about strength. A large bet on a wet, coordinated board is more polarising: it tends to mean either a genuinely strong hand or a draw with equity to back the aggression. Medium hands rarely want to build a big pot on scary textures.

The question to hold in your head is simple: which hands would play this way, and which hands would not? Every action your opponent takes eliminates some combinations and leaves others. That elimination is the entire game.

Bet sizing tells online

At lower stakes especially, bet sizes leak information. Many recreational players size up with strong hands and down with weak ones, purely out of instinct. Others use a small size with draws because they do not want to commit. You will not know which pattern a given player follows until you see a few showdowns — but once you do, that read is worth more than any hand-strength heuristic. Our guide to online poker strategy covers the fundamentals of bet sizing from the other side of the table.

Turn and river: where reads get made or broken

Most players do reasonable hand reading on the flop and then stop. The turn is where ranges narrow most sharply, because it is the street where medium hands give up and draws either commit or fold.

Ask two questions on every turn:

  • Did the card change anything? A blank turn means ranges stay roughly as they were. A card that completes an obvious draw, or a card that pairs the board, shifts both players' ranges immediately.
  • Would this opponent double-barrel with this hand? Many recreational players fire the flop with air and then shut down on the turn. If a player who never bets twice suddenly bets twice, believe them.

By the river, you should be able to name three or four specific combinations your opponent is most likely holding. If you cannot — if your read is a shrug — that is a sign to take the low-variance line rather than to invent a hero call.

A worked example

You hold ace-queen offsuit on the button. A tight regular opens from middle position and you call. Flop comes queen-eight-three rainbow. They bet small, you call. Turn is a five. They bet large. River is a seven and they shove.

Work the range. Their preflop open is tight. On a queen-high dry board, their small flop bet includes their entire range. The large turn bet on a blank narrows sharply — a tight player rarely fires big on a brick with a marginal hand. Then a river shove on another blank card. Which hands are doing this? Sets, and possibly ace-queen for a chopped pot or king-queen for a worse kicker. There are very few bluffs available, because the draws they would bluff with mostly do not exist on a rainbow board with no straight completions.

Top pair with a good kicker feels strong. Against that specific sequence from that specific player, it is a fold. That is hand reading — arriving at a decision that contradicts your gut because the evidence points one way.

How to practise

Hand reading improves through deliberate repetition, not through volume alone:

  • Pick one opponent per session and narrate their range out loud on every street, even in hands you are not in.
  • Review hands you lost at showdown and ask at which street the read was available.
  • Keep notes. Online sites let you tag players; a note like fires turn only with two pair plus is worth a buy-in later.
  • Play fewer tables. You cannot read ranges properly while managing six tables at once, and the extra hands per hour do not compensate for worse decisions.

If you are playing in a regulated province, table conditions matter too — a softer lineup gives you more readable opponents and faster learning. The habit that pays

Hand reading is slow at first and then becomes automatic. The players who never develop it stay stuck at breakeven for years, blaming variance for outcomes their own decisions produced. The ones who practise it stop needing to guess. Every extra street of accurate narrowing turns a coin-flip decision into an obvious one, and obvious decisions are where poker profit lives.
